brief: Three-step mobile onboarding carousel with illustration area, headline, body copy, pagination dots, and CTA. Knobs: step count, active step, accent color, dot style, and skip-link toggle. Price: 9

flaws: The faded side phones push body copy and the 'Skip'/'Back' links to very low contrast. In the default and light-brand renders the secondary-screen text is barely legible. It reads as a depth effect, but a designer pasting the asset into a deck gets greyed-out copy they cannot use.
Preset Iris is pixel-identical to the defaults, so it wastes a preset slot and shows no range.
At maximum step count the layout drops from three phones to two, offset as a pair. The active step is shown at full size, but steps 1–3 disappear entirely, so the 'carousel' framing weakens.
The illustrations are fixed per step, and no knob swaps or tints them independently of the accent. In the dark probe the purple secondary in the illustrations is hard-coded, not brand-derived.
grades.lesson: When you de-emphasise secondary elements (inactive screens, background cards), use scale, position, blur or a uniform overlay rather than fading text colour. Keep any text that remains visible at legible contrast in every brand theme. Also check that each preset differs visibly from the defaults before shipping it.

brief: Multi-tier pricing comparison table with feature checkmark rows and a highlighted plan. Knobs: tier count (2-4), featured tier, monthly/annual toggle state, feature row count, and accent color. Price: 8

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: radius

flaws: Light brand probe: the table surface barely separates from the cream page, and the featured card's tinted fill turns a muddy grey-green instead of reading as a clean highlight.
Secondary text is very small and low-contrast at the rendered size, notably the 'billed yearly' lines, tier taglines and dashes. It is borderline on the dark surfaces.

The featured card's overhang is asymmetric. It rises well above the table top but drops only a few pixels below the bottom edge, so at defaults the lower edge looks slightly unresolved rather than deliberate.
Within the featured column, the Priority support row shows a dash while the tier to its right has a check. This is a content issue, but it weakens the highlighted plan in the demo.
Knobs cover the brief, but there is no knob for highlight style or for hiding the badge.
grades.lesson: Derive container and highlight surface tones from the page background with an enforced minimum contrast step, rather than from fixed tints or alpha overlays, so cards stay distinct and highlights stay clean on any brand palette.

brief: Clean A4/Letter invoice with header logo slot, client block, line-item table, tax and total rows. Knobs: accent color, font pairing, row count, paid/unpaid stamp toggle, and currency format. Price: 6

flaws: The paid state is stated four times: the header pill, the rubber stamp, the 'Amount paid / Received' block and the 'Total paid' bar. This redundancy dilutes hierarchy, and the skeuomorphic stamp will read as dated to some buyers.
At default row count there is a large dead zone between the notes/stamp and the footer. Nothing absorbs the space, so the lower third feels unfinished.

At maximum rows the table compresses its row height to roughly 60% of default rather than keeping a consistent rhythm. The table looks denser and cheaper than the default state. There is also no overflow or continuation pattern beyond 14 items.
Studio and Forest differ from the default only in accent and paper tint. Font pairing, currency format and the unpaid state are never shown in any render, so the most distinctive knobs are unproven.
Footer labels and the stamp date are very small. They are legible in print but marginal on screen previews.
grades.lesson: When a toggle expresses a state (paid, overdue, draft), surface it once at the highest-hierarchy position and let other components stay neutral. Repeating the same signal across several elements reads as noise, not emphasis.

brief: Thermal-style receipt with a torn zigzag edge, monospace line items, and an optional barcode. Knobs: paper tint, item count, tear-edge depth, barcode or QR toggle, and footer message. Price: 0

flaws: The date ring inside the PAID stamp is about 6px. It is illegible in every render and reads as noise rather than detail.
At 14 items the whole receipt is scaled down to fit the frame instead of growing. All type gets noticeably smaller and the top tear edge sits close to the frame edge.
The QR state of the barcode/QR toggle appears in no render, so it cannot be verified.
The dark brand probe inverts the paper to near-black with white print. It is legible but loses the thermal-paper metaphor, and the inverted barcode looks less convincing.
There is no knob for the store name/header text or for rotation. A designer will almost always want to rebrand 'OASIS MARKET' and control the tilt.
grades.lesson: Any decorative micro-text, like text inside stamps, seals or badges, must render at a legible minimum size at defaults and at max-density scales. Otherwise drop it. Unreadable filler reads as noise and cheapens an otherwise polished asset.

brief: Settings page with grouped rows, toggles, selects, and section headers. Knobs: row count per group, toggle on/off states, theme mode, density (compact/comfortable), and sidebar toggle. Price: 7

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: ink

flaws: Light brand probe: the cards, search field and Cancel button are tinted a beige that is the same as or slightly darker than the cream canvas. Raised surfaces recede instead of lifting, card edges blur, and secondary description text loses contrast.
The Danger Zone stays a single row at every row count. At defaults and especially at max rows, this leaves a large empty bottom-right quadrant and unbalances the two-column grid.
The density and sidebar-toggle knobs promised in the brief are not clearly demonstrated in any render. The max render combines row count and density, so neither can be verified on its own.
Row description text is very small and light grey. It is borderline for legibility, especially on the tinted light probe.
grades.lesson: When deriving surface tokens from a brand background, enforce a minimum luminance step and a fixed direction. In light themes, cards and inputs must be lighter than the canvas. This keeps elevation and text contrast intact on tinted backgrounds.

brief: Sign-in screen with email and password fields, generic social-auth buttons, and a split-image or centered-card layout. Knobs: layout variant, brand color, error state toggle, remember-me checkbox, and dark mode. Price: 0

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: remember

flaws: Ember preset: the default focused password field gets a red-orange ring, and 'Forgot password?' turns the same red-orange. This reads as a validation error on an untouched form. The focus state is indistinguishable from what an error state would look like, which is a real usability problem on a sign-in screen whose brief includes an error toggle.
The brief asks for an error-state toggle and a split-or-centered-card layout variant, but no render shows either. The two most important knobs cannot be verified.

Max-range render: the floating decorative dots collapse into a cluster near the ring centre and read as stray specks. The rings shift off-centre so the art panel loses its composition rather than intensifying it.
The art panel at defaults is generic concentric rings on a gradient. The upper half is empty space with three arbitrary dots, so the panel carries little intent beyond filling space.
The password field is shown focused with a caret at defaults. That is a demo state rather than a clean resting state, and it makes the brand-colour collision above more visible.
The dark brand probe holds up well (lime button with dark label, legible fields), but the footer and helper text there are very low contrast against near-black.
grades.lesson: Never derive focus, active or selection styling from the brand colour alone. Keep error and success colours as fixed semantic tokens, and test a red or orange brand to confirm that 'focused' and 'invalid' still look different at a glance.

flaws: Dark brand probe: the illustration panel is a huge field of saturated lime with a lavender sun and periwinkle waves. The palette reads like a hue-rotation accident, not a design decision. It clashes hard with the dark form side. A senior designer could not ship a dark-mode sign-in where the hero panel is the brightest, loudest thing on screen.
Dark brand probe: the lime panel overpowers the near-black form column, so the screen's visual weight is inverted for a dark theme.
The max-knob render barely differs from defaults: slightly pill-shaped controls and marginally taller waves. Either the knob ranges are timid or important knobs aren't exposed for testing.

Two briefed knobs never appear in any render: the centered-card layout variant and the error-state toggle. Their quality can't be verified, and the error state is a core requirement for a sign-in asset.

Ember preset: 'Forgot password?' and 'Create an account' drop to a near-black or brown tone, unlike the other presets where they use the brand colour. The link treatment is inconsistent across themes.
Minor: the testimonial uses straight-looking quotation marks instead of typographic quotes.
grades.lesson: When a decorative palette is derived from the brand colour, build it from tints and shades of the brand hue, anchored to the current mode's surface colour. Never use complementary or rotated hues. Always test with a high-chroma brand on dark mode, so the hero art can't outshine the UI or produce clashing hue pairs.

brief: Checkout screen with card form, order summary, and pay button. Knobs: accent color, card network chip style, light/dark mode, field corner radius, number of line items, and currency symbol. Price: 8

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: chipStyle

flaws: The order summary math is wrong at every setting. The Ceramic Mug and Field Notebook carry quantity badges of 2 and 3, and the header counts quantities (6 items at defaults, 9 at max). But each line shows a single-unit price, and the subtotal is just those unit prices added up ($68+$48+$48 = $164). With those quantities the true subtotal would be $308. On a checkout template, totals that don't reconcile would embarrass a designer in any stakeholder review.
Quantity badges are inconsistent. Some items show a count and others show none, so the 1x items look unlabeled rather than deliberately quiet.

At the max preset, the Mug and Notebook thumbnails render as dark, desaturated tiles with the badges crowding them. They no longer match the accent-tinted thumbnails on the other rows, so the list looks patchy.

In the light brand probe, the card art and the mug thumbnail render salmon/orange while the accent is teal. In the dark probe, the card and mug are purple while the accent is lime. These decorative fills ignore the brand colour, so the screen looks two-branded.

Two knobs from the brief show no visible effect in any render. The currency symbol is '$' everywhere and the card network chip is always the same VISA badge. Field corner radius barely changes the inputs at max. These knobs either do nothing or were never exercised, so I can't verify they work.
In dark mode, the small helper text ('or pay with card', the encryption note, the footer links) drops to very low contrast. It is close to illegible at the rendered size.
grades.lesson: Placeholder data in a template must stay internally consistent under every knob setting. If you show quantities, prices and totals, derive them from one source (line total = unit price × quantity; subtotal = sum of line totals; header count = sum of quantities), so the numbers never contradict each other at defaults or at any preset.

flaws: The field corner radius knob appears to do almost nothing. At 'every range knob at maximum', the inputs, card field and pay button look the same as the default, so the knob's range is too narrow to justify exposing it.
The decorative credit-card mockup is jammed into the top-right of the form column. It crowds the 'Payment' heading, nearly touches the top edge and the column divider, and adds no information.
Card-network branding is redundant. A VISA/MC/AMEX chip row sits above the card field and another VISA badge sits inside it, which adds noise to the most important input.

'Wallet Pay' and 'Pay later' are styled as a segmented selection with a heavy black active state, then followed by 'or pay with card'. It is unclear whether they are express-pay buttons or tabs. The black fill also competes with the accent pay button for primary emphasis.
The currency symbol knob is never exercised in any render, and every view shows '$' and 'USD'. There is no evidence that non-USD symbols, longer codes or symbol placement hold up.
The design is a generic Stripe-style checkout with little distinctive point of view. It is competent, but there is not much a designer couldn't assemble from an existing UI kit.
grades.lesson: Make every exposed knob's extreme visibly different from its default, and verify this in the max-range render. A knob whose range produces no perceptible change is clutter that erodes buyer trust in all the other controls.

brief: Credit-card-ratio gift card with amount, recipient line, and decorative background. Knobs: denomination, gradient or pattern fill, foil-shine overlay, corner radius, and front/back view. Price: 5

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: ink

flaws: Both brand probes fall apart. The teal→coral (light) and lime→violet (dark) gradients interpolate through a muddy grey-brown/grey-green midpoint, so the cards look dirty rather than branded.

In the dark brand probe, the ribbon recolours to a saturated cyan that clashes with the lime and violet fill. With the cheap-looking gradient, the card reads as a garish default instead of an intentional design.
In the light brand probe, the yellow-gold ribbon sits on coral with weak separation, and the bow loses definition.
The 'Nº 0482' serial and the 'TO' label are tiny and lose contrast on the darker or saturated ends of the brand gradients.
The brief promises a pattern fill option and a front/back view, but no render shows either. The back face is unverified, so a buyer has no evidence these knobs work or look designed.
The max-knob render barely differs from the defaults apart from the corner radius and a $500 amount. Foil-shine at maximum is not visibly stronger, so the range of that knob is questionable.
The bow is decent but generic. Its inner loop shading reads as flat dark blobs at this size, and the ribbon position is fixed, so there is little compositional flexibility.
The recipient line is an empty rule with no sample name state. Designers can't see how a real name sits on the line.
grades.lesson: When a component takes arbitrary brand colours into a gradient, interpolate in a perceptual space (e.g. OKLCH) or insert a controlled midpoint stop. Also derive accent and foreground colours from contrast against the actual local background, so complementary brand pairs don't collapse into a muddy grey middle with clashing accents.

flaws: Light brand probe: the fill becomes a teal-to-mustard-to-orange gradient across unrelated hues. It reads muddy and dated rather than premium. The dark bronze ribbon sinks into it and the orange wave lines look like noise.
Dark brand probe: a neon lime-cyan-violet gradient clashes with the dark page. The magstripe turns olive-brown and looks wrong. The grey '$50' and teal ribbon lose punch, so the luxury feel is gone.
The back card's value seal is half-covered by the front card in every render. Its amount ('$50' / '$500') is clipped, which looks like a stacking accident rather than a deliberate overlap.
'Nº 0482' at the bottom right is tiny and loses contrast on the orange end of the light probe gradient.
Every render shows the front/back stack, so it is unclear whether the brief's front/back view knob can isolate a single face. A designer wanting just the front card has no visible path.
At maximum corner radius the cards look like rounded badges rather than credit-card ratio cards, so the radius range runs too far.
grades.lesson: When deriving a fill from brand colours, build a tonal ramp within one hue family (lighter and darker shades of the brand colour) instead of a multi-stop gradient between unrelated hues. Cross-hue gradients turn muddy or neon with arbitrary brand inputs and destroy the premium finish the asset depends on.

brief: Donut chart with segment labels, center total, and legend. Knobs: segment values, ring thickness, gap between segments, palette, center text, and legend position. Price: 0

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: ink, caption

flaws: At maximum ring thickness the centre hole gets cramped. '1,220' nearly spans the hole, and the caption wraps awkwardly to 'Total spend' / '($k)' at a reduced size. It stays legible but no longer looks designed.

Some adjacent segments are hard to tell apart. In Ember, Sales and Support are both yellow-orange; in the dark probe, Marketing and Sales are similar teals; in defaults, Engineering and Marketing are similar blues. Legend-to-segment matching relies too much on position.

The legend-position knob is only ever shown on the right, and segment values are never pushed to a stressful case, such as a 1–2% sliver or more segments. That leaves leader-label collision handling unverified.

Percentages use largest-remainder rounding: Design shows 35% although 420/1220 is 34.4%. This is defensible so the total reaches 100%, but it is undocumented and could confuse users who check the maths.
grades.lesson: When a knob shrinks the space available to embedded text, such as a donut hole or a card body, define an explicit fallback. For example, drop the secondary caption below a size threshold rather than letting it wrap and shrink, so extreme settings still look deliberate.

brief: Dashboard data table with sortable headers, status pills, avatar cells, row selection, and pagination. Knobs: row and column count, zebra striping, density, selected rows, and status color mapping. Price: 9

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: ink

flaws: Studio preset: the grey selected-row tint is only slightly darker than the zebra stripe. Without the checkbox, selected and striped rows are hard to tell apart.

At max, selected rows equals every visible row, so the whole table turns lavender. Zebra striping and row separation vanish, and the extreme reads as one flat block rather than a useful selected state.
The column-count range is narrow. Maxing it adds only a single Usage column, so the 'column count' knob barely stretches the layout and never tests truncation of long values.
Row count tops out at 12 and density shows no visible change at max. There is no evidence the compact or comfortable extremes were exercised, so dense-dashboard use is unproven.
Status colour mapping is not demonstrated beyond the default four states. No render shows a custom or remapped palette.
grades.lesson: Selected-row state must remain distinguishable from zebra striping by more than a small luminance step, especially in monochrome themes. Pair the selected tint with a second cue, such as a leading accent bar or a stronger tint, and verify that both alternating and selected rows survive when the selection count covers every visible row.

brief: Oasis Town kit: an isometric park diorama matching oasis-town.mjs: a round fountain built from boxes and water quads, paths, benches, lamp posts, many cubic trees, a playground slide. Knobs: tree colours by season, water colour, path colour, time with glowing lamps, tree density, seed. price 7

flaws: Dark brand probe breaks semantics. The fountain water turns neon lime and reads as grass or slime, not water. The paths go near-black, so they disappear into the dark background and lose any sense of being walkways.

The 'time with glowing lamps' knob shows no visible effect in any render. The max-range shot and the dark probe both have unlit lamp posts and daytime lighting, so a headline knob from the brief is either broken or imperceptible.

At max density, trees clump and interpenetrate each other with no spacing logic. Crowns pile into the fountain area and crowd lamps and benches, and some trees sit right on the platform edge. The result reads as random scatter, not a planted park.
At defaults, the pink tree's crown overlaps the fountain's white rim blocks, and a lamp post butts into the basin. These are visible intersections in the hero render.
The season knob does not read as a season at max. It gives a random mix of pink and green crowns rather than a coherent spring, autumn or winter palette.
Usefulness is narrow for a product designer: a single fixed-camera isometric park vignette with limited composition control (no framing, scale or element toggles).
grades.lesson: When mapping brand colours onto an illustration, bind each colour to a semantic role with guarded hue and contrast ranges (e.g. water stays blue-cyan, paths keep contrast against both ground and background) rather than pouring raw brand accents into whatever slot is free. Then verify that every knob listed in the brief produces a visible change at its extremes.

flaws: At maximum tree density, trees spill onto the paths and the fountain plaza ring. In the bottom quadrant two cherry trees sit right against the fountain on the walkway, and the evergreens crowd the path edges. The scatter does not respect the layout.
Trees and lamp posts overlap at defaults. The top-centre lamp post punches through the cherry tree behind it, which reads as a collision, not depth.
Max-density trees clump into overlapping clusters (left quadrant), while other zones stay sparse. Placement looks random, not designed.
The season knob is never shown working. Every render is the same cherry-blossom pink, so the headline 'tree colours by season' feature is unverified.

The presets barely differ. Lagoon only shifts the water hue, and Candy only recolours the paths and benches. The light brand probe is nearly identical to Lagoon. These are weak demonstrations of range.
Lamps glow at full intensity even in daytime renders, which undercuts the 'time with glowing lamps' knob.
In the dark probe the grass stays fairly bright and the lamp glow is subtle, so the night mood is only half-committed.
grades.lesson: Any scattered or density-driven element must be placed against an exclusion map of every other footprint (paths, props, focal objects, each other), and must be checked at maximum density, where collisions first become visible.

brief: Vertical or horizontal bar chart with axis, gridlines, labels, and tooltip callout. Knobs: data values, orientation, grouped/stacked mode, bar radius, palette, and gridline toggle. Price: 0

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: title, gridlines

flaws: At the max-knob render the tooltip anchor dot floats to the right of the Jun Series A bar instead of sitting on its top edge. The marker position is not recomputed when bar radius or geometry changes, so the callout points at empty space. This is a broken render.

At max radius the bars become full pill caps. The rounded tops sit well above the true value line, so readers can no longer tell where a bar ends (e.g. Jun at 88 reads ambiguously against the 80/100 gridlines). The radius range should be capped relative to bar width or value precision.
The bare 'Grouped' text at bottom right reads like a leaked state or debug label. It is not styled as a toggle or legend item and has no clear purpose in a static deliverable.

None of the renders shows the horizontal orientation, stacked mode or gridline-off state promised in the brief. Half of the knob surface is unverified, and nothing suggests those modes were designed with care.

The headline '570 total' sums both series with no indication of that. 'Monthly revenue' has no unit or currency, and the y-axis is unlabeled. This is weak data semantics for a revenue chart a designer would drop into a product.
The tooltip is pinned to the tallest grouped bar and only lists the values. It offers no delta or total, so it adds little beyond what the axis already shows.
grades.lesson: Derive every annotation's anchor (tooltip pointer, marker dot, highlight band) from the same computed geometry as the shape it annotates, and re-render at every knob extreme to confirm the annotation still touches its target.

flaws: The tooltip completely hides May's Online bar in the defaults, every preset and both brand probes. In the max-knob render it hides the top of May's Online bar. A reader can't see one of the six primary data points in any shipped state.
The tooltip also covers the top half of the hovered group's own Retail bar (Apr, $40k). The callout obscures the data it is describing.

The tooltip is anchored to the Online bar top and always extends right, with no awareness of neighbouring bar heights. In the max render it flips left only because it hits the edge, and still lands on data.

The 'every range knob at its maximum' render is nearly identical to the defaults. Bar radius, spacing and values look unchanged, and only the highlighted month moves. The range knobs are either too timid or not wired, so their maximums show no intentional change.

None of the renders shows the knobs promised in the brief: horizontal orientation, stacked mode or the gridline toggle. There is no evidence these states are handled, especially stacked mode, where tooltip and label collisions are most likely.
In the dark probe, the hover highlight band is almost invisible against the near-black background, so the selected-column affordance disappears.

The large empty plot area above the bars (nothing tops out above about $88k on a $100k axis) combined with a crowded tooltip region makes the layout feel unbalanced. The axis max could be tighter, or the callout could sit in that headroom.
grades.lesson: Treat callouts and tooltips as layout that must not hide data. Position them by measuring every mark in the plot, not just the anchored one. Prefer empty headroom above the series, flip sides or shift vertically when they would cover any bar or point, and check each preset and extreme specifically for data hidden under overlays.

brief: Oasis Town kit: an isometric little train station diorama matching oasis-town.mjs: a platform with a canopy, a short two-car train on rails, a ticket booth, benches, a station clock pole, a vending machine. Knobs: train colour (primary role), canopy colour, cars count, time with lit windows, season, seed. price 10

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: name

flaws: A cherry tree at the front-left corner stands directly on the rail track in every render, including defaults. Decorative scatter ignores functional zones.
At max range, the station-name sign in the middle of the platform turns into a yellow cluster tangled with the passenger figures. It reads as a glitch, not a sign.
The station-name text ('Hanamachi') is illegible at the default render size. It is a noisy smudge rather than a usable label.
Brief elements are missing or unreadable: no vending machine is visibly identifiable, and benches cannot be distinguished from the figures.
The time-of-day (lit windows) and season knobs show no visible effect. Every render has daytime and cherry blossoms, so those knobs are either unproven or non-functional.
The presets barely differ. Seaside and the light brand probe are near-identical, and Tokaido only swaps two hues. Presets offer no real range.
In the dark brand probe, the lime-green train and violet canopy sit on a stark white platform, and the cherry blossoms stay unchanged. The palette clashes and looks unconsidered rather than branded.
The composition sits low-right with a large dead area at top-left. At max the elongated diorama pushes the clock pole and canopy against the edges, giving uneven framing.
grades.lesson: Procedural scatter (trees, props, figures, signage) must be placed against explicit exclusion zones derived from the functional geometry (tracks, paths, walkways, labels). Those zones must be recomputed whenever a knob changes the layout's length or count, so nothing ever sits on, through or tangled with a primary element.

flaws: At max range the canopy grows but the cherry-blossom props do not move to make room. Pink cubes poke through and sit on the canopy's back edge, and a row of white/pink blocks crowds under the roofline. It reads as geometry clipping, not trees behind a roof.
At max range the left-hand tree cluster piles into the ticket booth roof and the platform corner. The booth looks squeezed and the composition turns cluttered and lopsided.
The station sign at max range does not scale with the longer platform. 'Hanamachi' becomes a tiny label lost on a huge canopy.

No render shows the 'time with lit windows' knob or a non-spring season. The dark brand probe still shows unlit train and booth windows, and every render has the same cherry blossoms. Two of the six briefed knobs either do nothing visible or are unproven.
The station name 'Hanamachi' is hardcoded. For a product designer, the station sign is the obvious thing to replace with their own copy, but there is no text knob.

In the dark brand probe, the primary-role train colour turns neon lime against the purple canopy and dark ground. It is legible, but there is no tonal adjustment, so the train vibrates against the scene instead of sitting in it.
The presets only swap canopy and train hues plus the background tint. Composition, car count, time and season are never varied, so the presets show almost none of the asset's range.
grades.lesson: When a count or size knob grows a central structure, regenerate the placement of decorative scatter (trees, props, signage) against the new footprint. Add collision checks so props never intersect the structure, and scale key labels with the structure.

brief: Oasis Town kit: an isometric food-truck plaza diorama matching oasis-town.mjs: 2-4 food trucks with serving hatches and striped awnings, picnic benches, string lights, a few cubic trees and planters on a paved slab. Knobs: truck colours via roles, truck count, time (night lights), season, seed. price 8

flaws: String-light poles stand directly in front of each truck. In isometric view they slice through the serving hatches and striped awnings, which are the hero detail the brief asks for.
The front-left shade sails overlap into a confusing cluster of flat triangles. They read as floating paper rather than tensioned shades, and the overlap gets worse at max range.
The layout is identical across Picnic, Riviera and both brand probes. Presets are only palette swaps, and seed and season show no visible effect, so the composition has very little range.
In the dark brand probe the paving becomes a harsh black/charcoal checkerboard that competes with the trucks. Benches and planters stay in their light-mode tones and look pasted in.
The dark probe pairs lime trucks with saturated purple and cyan sails. The garish combination is unflattering, with no tonal moderation of brand colours for dark backgrounds.
The diorama sits low-right with a large dead area top-left, so the framing feels unconsidered.
grades.lesson: In isometric scenes, reserve a clearance zone in front of every focal object and keep vertical props such as poles and posts out of it. Occluders in projection always cut across the feature the viewer most needs to read.

flaws: Roadside cubic trees sit directly behind the trucks and poke out above their roofs. At default and max they read as trees growing on top of the trucks, especially on the third truck with its rooftop box and on the second truck at max.
Picnic and Riviera presets change only hue. Layout, time, season, umbrella count and props are identical, so the presets show no meaningful range.
The season knob has no visible effect in any render. Foliage is the same green in every image, so a promised knob is either missing or too weak to notice.
At max truck count, the trucks, people and benches crowd into one overlapping band along the road. Tiny figures merge into truck fronts and the scene loses its readable spacing.
Figures are minuscule and few at default. The plaza reads as an empty set rather than a lively venue, which weakens its value as a hero or spot illustration.
String lights are thin and nearly invisible in daytime renders. The brief lists them as a feature, but they only register in the dark probe.
Niche, fixed-composition subject. Beyond recolouring there is little a product designer can adapt for different layouts or crops.
grades.lesson: In isometric scenes, keep tall background props out of the silhouette of foreground objects, or offset them clearly so they cannot be misread as stacked on top. Overlapping depth layers that align vertically read as one object.

brief: Responsive top navigation bar with logo slot, links, search, and avatar or CTA. Knobs: link count, active item, sticky blur background, alignment, mobile hamburger view, and theme mode. Price: 0

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: ink

flaws: At max knobs the active item ('Company') loses its pill background and is shown only as bolder text. The active state renders differently depending on which link is selected, so the active-item knob is unreliable.
The nav overlaps and hides the top card of the hero dashboard in every render. Instead of reading as a frosted bar over content, it looks like a clipped layout collision.
The 'frosted' effect named in the title is not visible. The bar reads as a near-opaque panel, and nothing behind it shows through blurred, so the sticky blur knob shows no visible change.
The mobile hamburger view and the alignment knob, both in the brief, appear in none of the renders. Their range is unverified.
At six links the centre group crowds against the collapsed search and CTA, leaving little breathing room before the right cluster.
grades.lesson: Make every state a knob can select (active, hover, selected) come from one style rule applied by index, and render the first, middle and last options. A state that only looks right at its default position is a bug buyers will find immediately.

flaws: The nav itself, which is the actual asset, takes up a thin strip of the frame. The hero and dashboard mockup dominate, and the nav labels are tiny at the default render size.

The 'every knob at maximum' render shows link count, active item and the search collapse working well. Alignment and sticky-blur strength look unchanged from defaults, so two of the brief's knobs show no visible effect at their extremes.
The desktop right cluster stacks search, CTA and avatar, even though the brief says avatar *or* CTA. The avatar sits tight against the nav's right edge.
In the mobile header, the avatar is crammed against the close button with almost no gap.
The decorative frosted blob behind the desktop nav reads as a stray hard-edged shape near the browser chrome rather than clearly as content scrolling under glass.
grades.lesson: Every knob in the brief should produce a visibly different render at its extreme. If alignment or blur strength looks identical at max, the knob is either broken or too subtle to sell, so widen its range or make its effect legible in the preview.

brief: Task card for kanban boards with title, tags, assignee avatars, due date, and progress. Knobs: tag colors, priority indicator, avatar count, checklist progress, cover-image toggle, and column header. Price: 5

flaws: Light brand probe: the 'AK' avatar puts white initials on a bright cyan fill. That is roughly 1.7:1 contrast, and the 12px initials are barely legible. The progress bar was darkened to a deeper teal for this probe, but the avatar fills still use the raw brand tint, so contrast handling is inconsistent across elements.
Light brand probe: the cover's central phone uses white UI marks on pale cyan and nearly disappears. The hero illustration loses its focal point.
Dark brand probe: the middle 'MJ' avatar has dark initials on a mid-green fill with marginal contrast, and the overlapping avatars read as a muddy cluster.

The 'every range knob at max' render changes only the avatar overflow (+3) and the checklist (8/8 complete). The priority indicator shows 'High' in every render, so the other priority levels and the cover-off layout were never shown.
The column header count stays '3' and the comment count stays '4' in every render. These look hardcoded, not knob-driven.
The description wraps at about 60% of the card width, leaving a large dead area to its right at defaults.
grades.lesson: Never reuse the brand accent as a text-bearing fill without checking contrast: for every surface that holds text or icons (avatars, badges, illustration details), compute the foreground from the actual fill colour against a minimum contrast ratio. Do not assume one fixed light/dark choice works for all brands.

flaws: The middle avatar (MJ) uses white initials on a light tint of the accent, so its contrast is roughly 2:1 or worse. It is hard to read in defaults (lavender), Meadow (mint), Sunset (salmon) and especially the light brand probe (bright cyan).
In the dark brand probe the same avatar flips to dark initials on dark olive, which is also low contrast. The avatar text colour is clearly fixed per slot rather than computed against its fill.

In the light brand probe the generated 'Design' tag (coral fill, red text) lands on almost the same hue as the 'High' priority pill. A category label and a priority signal then read as the same thing.
In the dark brand probe the lime bars and pills on the lime side phones sit on a dark olive cover with weak separation, so the cover illustration turns muddy.
No render shows the cover-image toggle switched off, so the card's no-cover layout cannot be verified.
Column header count stays at '3' at every setting and the header knob shows no visible variation. Its range is unproven.
grades.lesson: Never hard-code foreground colour per element when the background is derived from a theme or brand colour. Compute text colour from the actual fill's contrast (target ≥4.5:1 for small text) so every generated tint stays legible in light and dark brands. Also keep semantic colours like priority or status in hue families that tag palettes are barred from reusing.

brief: Drag-and-drop upload area with a file list showing progress bars and success/error rows. Knobs: dropzone state (idle, hover, uploading), file count, progress values, border dash style, and accent color. Price: 0

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: border

flaws: Midnight preset: the 'Attach 1 file' label on the light periwinkle button appears low-contrast, likely below 4.5:1. The dark brand probe correctly flips to dark text on lime, so the text-colour switch point seems mis-tuned for mid-luminance accents.
Dark-mode error row: red helper text on a dark red-brown tint is muted and harder to read than the rest of the list.
Every render shows the 'uploading' dropzone state with a dashed border, so the idle and hover states and the dash-style range could not be checked.
Minor data inconsistencies: the max render shows 1.2 of 2.8 MB as 42% (should round to 43%), and the default dropzone total of 3.4 MB does not match the row values, which sum to 3.5 MB.
At max file count the dropzone shrinks to make room. It still reads as intentional, but the modal sits close to the frame bottom, so a higher count would likely overflow without a scroll treatment.
grades.lesson: When auto-picking text colour on an accent fill, choose it by computed contrast ratio against both candidates (white vs. dark) rather than a fixed luminance cutoff, and test mid-luminance pastels like periwinkle and sky blue, where fixed cutoffs fail most often.

brief: Smooth or straight-segment line chart with area fill, data points, and a hover marker. Knobs: series count, data values, curve tension, gradient area fill, point visibility, and axis labels. Price: 6

flaws: Max-knob render has a collision. The November tooltip sits low and left of the hover line, directly over the Organic hover marker at 3,730. The active point is half-buried under the tooltip's top-right corner, and the Sep–Nov stretch of the Organic line runs behind the tooltip. The tooltip hides the exact data it is reporting.

Tooltip placement ignores where the series actually are at the hovered index. In the defaults the empty space below the lines happened to be free; with three series spread across the plot, the same logic lands on data.

The YTD delta pill is a hardcoded green tint. It does not adapt to the theme, so in Midnight and the dark brand probe it is dark green on near-black with weak contrast. The '+16.7% YTD' text is hard to read at a glance.
On dark themes the secondary labels ('Direct traffic · Dec', axis ticks, month labels) are dim grey on near-black. Their contrast is marginal for real dashboard use.
Dark brand probe: the lime-over-purple area fill blends into a muddy olive band between the lines. It reads as dirty rather than as a deliberate tint.
At maximum the series knob only reaches 3 series, which is thin for a general-purpose line chart.
None of the renders shows straight-segment mode, points hidden, or axis labels off, though all are promised in the brief. The core 'smooth or straight' claim is unverified.
grades.lesson: Position floating overlays such as tooltips and callouts against the actual content at the hover point, not against a fixed offset. Compute the bounding box of every active marker and every nearby line segment, then flip or shift the overlay until it touches none of them. Verify this at maximum series count, where the free space is smallest.

flaws: At maximum series count the legend wraps unevenly. 'Benchmark' sits alone on a second row, right-aligned under Referral and Social, which reads as overflow rather than intentional layout.
At max the y-axis domain extends to 15k while the data peaks around 8.2k. The top half of the plot is empty and the five series are crushed into the lower band, so their crossings are hard to read.
In the max render the Referral and Social series are both dotted and separated only by hue (deep purple vs teal). This is weak differentiation with no fallback for colour-blind viewers.
Hover points at November in the max render cluster around 5–6k (Social, Benchmark), so the grey and teal markers nearly stack.
In the dark brand probe the lime area gradient turns muddy olive against near-black. The purple secondary line also has noticeably lower contrast than the primary.
The area fill and headline metric only ever bind to the first series. There is no visible way to make the hero number reflect another series or to fill secondary series.
grades.lesson: When a knob adds items to a shared row (legend entries, tabs, chips), design the overflow state deliberately: balanced wrapping, a column grid, or relocation below the plot. Never let items spill one-by-one onto an orphaned line.

brief: Audio player card with album art, track info, scrubber, and transport controls. Knobs: size (mini/full), progress position, waveform or bar scrubber, art gradient, and play/pause state. Price: 6

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: ink, playing

flaws: At max progress the remaining-time label drops its sign ('0:00' instead of '−0:00'). The time readout is inconsistent at the extreme.
At 100% progress the playhead sits flush on the last waveform bar at the right content edge. It reads as cramped instead of resolved.
None of the renders show the size (mini), scrubber-style (bar) or play-state knobs, so those variants are unverified. Only progress and colour were exercised.
The album art is a generic gradient with rings and grain. It is competent but undifferentiated, and in the lime dark probe the highlights wash out slightly.
Shuffle and repeat are muted grey with no visible on or off state, so they read as disabled instead of toggleable.
grades.lesson: When a value is formatted at defaults, check it at both ends of its range. Signs, padding and labels like '−0:00' must stay consistent, and indicators like playheads need breathing room at 0% and 100%.

brief: Landing page hero with headline, subcopy, dual CTAs, and a product-shot or abstract visual area. Knobs: layout (left, center, split), background style, headline length, badge pill toggle, and accent color. Price: 10

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: radius

flaws: A hard vertical seam runs down the middle of every render at about x=268. The background glow is painted only into the left column and stops dead at the column edge, so the right half reads as a separate flat panel. This is clearest in Midnight and the dark brand probe, where the purple, green and teal blobs end on a straight line. It looks like a clipping bug, not a deliberate split.
The 'every range knob at maximum' render is pixel-for-pixel identical to the defaults. Either the range knobs do nothing or their maximum equals the default, so the parametric range is unproven.
The briefed layout variants (center and split) and the headline-length knob have no visible effect in any render. Every render is the same left-aligned composition.
The dashboard mock is very faint at this scale. The sidebar is placeholder bars, the stat labels are barely legible, and the chart's end dot sits right against the card's right edge.
The avatar stack beside 'Loved by 12,000+ product teams' is tiny and its initials are illegible.
For a $10 hero, nothing on offer goes beyond a standard SaaS template once the knobs are shown not to change the layout.
grades.lesson: Paint decorative backgrounds (glows, gradients, blobs) on the full-bleed root layer, never inside a single column, so they don't hard-clip at layout seams. Then verify that every declared knob produces a visibly different render at its extremes.

flaws: The 'every range knob at maximum' render is nearly identical to defaults. The only visible change is a slightly larger corner radius and bigger background blobs, so the range knobs barely change anything and their ranges are far too timid to justify parametrisation.

Every render shows the same split layout and the same headline. The brief's left and center layouts, headline-length variation and badge toggle never appear, so the core knobs cannot be shown to work.

The secondary accent is hardcoded rather than derived from the brand. In the dark brand probe, the lime brand sits beside a violet toast check and a violet bottom-right glow, and the two clash. In the light teal probe, an orange toast icon and peach glow carry over from the default purple theme.
In the light themes, the metric cards use a muddy mid-grey or beige fill on a white panel, which looks dated next to the otherwise clean UI.
The product mockup is very generic: a SaaS dashboard with three stat cards and an area chart. It gives buyers little reason to pay over free hero templates.
grades.lesson: Before shipping, render every knob at its minimum and maximum and diff them against the defaults. If an extreme is not visibly and meaningfully different, widen the range or cut the knob. Derive every secondary accent from the brand colour so brand swaps never leave orphaned hues.

brief: Dropdown notification panel with grouped items, unread dots, avatars, and action buttons. Knobs: item count, unread count, tabs (all/mentions), empty-state toggle, and theme mode. Price: 7

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: radius

flaws: At max density the action buttons switch from rounded rectangles to full pills. The same component changes shape language depending on item count.
At max, the inline Accept/Decline and Approve/Deny buttons push right up against the unread-dot column. The Decline/Deny edge nearly touches the dot.
At max unread every row gets the tinted background, so the tint stops separating anything. The Today and Earlier groups become one undifferentiated wash.
The light brand probe's unread tint is a fairly saturated cyan. It is louder than the other presets and competes with the content.
The empty-state toggle is in the brief but never rendered, so it cannot be verified.
grades.lesson: When a component reflows into a compact layout under load, keep its visual primitives (corner radius, button style) identical to the default. Reserve clearance for persistent indicator columns so inline controls never crowd them.

brief: Conversion funnel with tapered stages, percentages, and drop-off annotations. Knobs: stage count, values, taper style (smooth/stepped), orientation, palette, and label placement. Price: 7

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: ink

flaws: The funnel silhouette is a fixed decorative trumpet, not encoded from the data. At defaults the last stage is 3.4% of the first but still about 40% of its width. Steps that lose 55% and 60% look like near-identical narrowings, so the shape tells the viewer nothing a table wouldn't.

The drop-off annotations float in a detached column. Each leader line starts in empty space and ends at a dot, connecting to neither the funnel boundary nor the stage labels, so the eye can't tie '−55.1%' to the transition it describes.

At max stage count (7), the bottom stage runs to the canvas edge with no bottom margin. The funnel tip and the 'Advocates · 0.64%' label are effectively cropped. The layout does not reflow vertically for added stages.
The right third of the canvas is dead space below the header. The drop-off column ends around x=430 while 'Overall conversion' anchors the far right, so the header and body grids don't align.

In the light brand probe, the brand palette is applied as a categorical sequence (teal → green → olive → amber → coral). An ordered funnel reads as unrelated categories. There is no sequential ramp derivation from the brand colour.

The brief promises taper style (smooth/stepped), orientation and label placement. None are shown in any render, and the 'all knobs at max' render changes only stage count. The headline knobs are unverified, and orientation in particular is the knob most likely to break this layout.
At 7 stages, the stage bands and label blocks drift out of vertical registration toward the bottom. Labels sit increasingly low relative to their bands.
grades.lesson: In data visualisations, either derive the geometry from the data or make the decorative shape explicitly a knob. Lay out annotations by anchoring each one to the exact element it describes. Then verify that adding items reflows within fixed margins instead of extending past the canvas.

flaws: The stage colour ramp fades toward the background colour in every theme, so the smallest and most important stage is the least visible. It is a pale periwinkle stem on cream at defaults, dark violet on near-black in Midnight, and dark olive on near-black in the dark brand probe. The final 'Paid' or 'Advocates' stage nearly disappears.

Width is proportional to volume with no minimum width. At 7 stages the 0.64% 'Advocates' stage collapses to a hairline that barely reads as a shape. Realistic funnels with steeper drop-off would vanish entirely.
At 7 stages the right-hand drop-off column crowds. Each 'N lost' caption sits almost against the next pill, and the pill-plus-caption pairs stop reading as distinct annotations.
The secondary text is too small to read at the delivered size: the subtitle, the stage sub-labels ('Sign-ups · 44.9%') and the 'lost' counts are all tiny, low-contrast grey.

The drop-off pill colour loses its loss meaning in several themes. It is lavender in Ember, slate-navy in the dark brand probe and teal in Midnight. The red 'drop' signal only survives in the light themes.

Most of the promised knobs are not demonstrated in any render: taper style (smooth/stepped), orientation and label placement. The 'every range knob at max' render only changes stage count, so the behaviour of the other promised knobs is unverified.
The large empty block in the lower-left quadrant beneath the funnel stem leaves the composition left-top heavy, with the funnel and annotations pushed to one diagonal.
grades.lesson: When a sequential colour ramp encodes rank or size, anchor it so the step furthest from the base colour moves away from the surface colour, not toward it. Also check that the smallest or last element still meets a minimum contrast against the background in both light and dark themes.
